title: Does the hazard trap explain why learning fails among social peers?
question: Z found that learning pays among 11 non-social peers (+6.9) but not among 11 social peers (-2.8). AA found that a lone social agent barely learns with hazards (+1.1) and learns without them (+6.2): its non-moving actions (attack, share, signal) keep it inside hazards. This study asks whether removing hazards also lets social agents learn in groups.
background: Same design as Z: fixed dynamics (substeps=32, reset_each_decision, normalize with normalize_to='innate'), 12 agents and 24 food, all agents train together for 1500 ticks, agent 0 is tested frozen among its frozen peers on 8 held-out worlds against a fresh untrained group. social12 repeats Z's social condition on new seeds; *_nohazard sets n_hazard=0. No pilot was run. Interpretation rule, fixed in advance: the hazard trap explains the group failure if H47a and H47b are supported; other social effects remain if H47c is also supported. Seeds 870-881 and worlds 9700-9707 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: Without hazards, learning pays among social peers
Removing hazards raises the learning gain among social peers
Without hazards, social peers still gain less than non-social peers
Without hazards, learning does not raise the attack rate among social peers
